To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

reducing dietary CP and RUP levels by decreasing dietary RDP in the diet of high-producing dairy cows in early lactaton does not affect production performance, nutrient digestion, and ruminal fermentation, but improves the efficiency of N use by decreasing N excretion in the urine.

decreasing dietary CP and decreasing RDP with a constant concentration RUP in the diet of high-producing Holstein dairy cows in early lactations does not affect milk yield and composition but increases the efficiency of N use.

the concentration of dietary CP could be decreased to 14.8%, RDP could be decreased to approximately 9.3%, and RUP could be maintained at 5.0% of dietary DM without negatively impacting the performance and health of early-lactation Holstein cows.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of reducing the dietary CP level on production performance, digestibility, N utilization, and blood metabolite concentrations in high-producing dairy cows in early lactations.
the effects of dietary protein and energy on the production of milk and meat in dairy cattle.
the development of an effective strategy for improving N efficiency in dairy cows.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the study support the hypothesis that the efficiency of N retention can be improved by decreasing dietary CP with a constant level of RUP in early lactation dairy cows.

decreasing the concentration of dietary RDP with the constant concentration of RUP in rations for early-lactation cows improves N utilization efficiency and minimizes N excretion without affecting production performance and blood metabolites.

decreasing dietary CP by decreasing RDP and keeping a constant concentration of RUP in diets fed to early-lactation Holstein cows had no adverse effects on milk production and milk protein content and improved N efficiency.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

decreasing dietary CP and decreasing RDP levels with a constant concentration (5.5%) of RUP in the diet of early-lactation cows did not affect milk production, but it improved the efficiency of N use.

the dietary CP and RUP requirements of lactating dairy cows in the early lactation period are not linearly related to milk production and that dietary RDP can be reduced to 9% CP in the diet without affecting milk production, nutrient digestibility or blood metabolites, but with a decrease in N excretion.
the dietary protein concentration of 14.8%, 15.6%, and 16.4%, with 5.5, 5.5 and 5.5 percent of RUP, respectively, is adequate for early lactating dairy cows.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the level of RUP in the diet is more critical to optimize protein utilization in dairy cows than is the total CP content of the diet.
it is possible to reduce the dietary protein and RDP in ruminant diets without affecting production performance.
reducing dietary CP and RUP levels in the diets of high-yielding dairy cows in early lactations does not affect milk production performance but improves the N utilization efficiency.
